definition: Impetuous means acting quickly and rashly, without thinking things through.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word impetuous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know impetuous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: One impetuous bid — doubled on a whim in the auction's final minute — cost Serena the entire restoration budget.
Hasty is milder than impetuous — a hasty choice is rushed by the clock, while an impetuous one skips the thinking even with time to spare.
Reckless goes further than impetuous — the impetuous swimmer dives before thinking, while the reckless one dives knowing the rocks are there.

Headlong pictures the motion itself — plunging straight in, momentum doing the deciding, like a dive or a downhill charge. Impetuous judges the mind behind the act: the pause for thought was available and got skipped. A rockslide is headlong; only a person can be impetuous.

Impulsive points at the inner urge — a sudden want or whim obeyed on the spot, like blurting out a secret. Impetuous stresses the headlong force of the act itself, the lunge with no pause for thought. The urge is impulsive; the charging, unweighed act is impetuous.

Impetuous means acting quickly and rashly, without thinking things through.
The climbing school's first lesson targets impetuous beginners: the ones who see a handhold and lunge for it, halfway up the wall before anyone has checked a rope.
Strength they have, the instructor says; what they skip is the thinking.
Impetuous means acting on the surge of the moment — quickly, forcefully, and without weighing what follows.
It is about the missing pause: the impetuous move may even succeed, but nobody, including the mover, thought it through first.
Impetuous faults the missing pause before an act — sudden force, no forethought.
Its everyday twin impulsive (in this unit's reference list) stresses the inner urge; impetuous stresses the headlong energy of the act itself.
Both stop short of reckless, which knows the danger and charges anyway.

The house went on the market on a Thursday.
By Friday lunch, Teo had made an offer on it.
His sister begged him to sleep on it; the inspection window was three full weeks, and nothing obliged him to move at all.
Friends were careful with the word afterward, but the loan officer was not: the purchase had been impetuous, she said, and the paperwork proved it.
Teo had not been pressed for time.
He had simply declined to use any of it — no survey ordered, no budget drafted, no second visit.
The porch he loved at first sight turned out to be resting on two rotten beams and one coat of fresh paint.
